items.title: docs(benchmarks): drop the stale tracker numbers, add a CI guard
items.body:
Closes #120.

The repo was promoted from a private tracker and the `#N` numbers came with it. Most no longer resolve; several land on real but unrelated public issues, so a reader following one arrives somewhere plausible and false. The mix is what makes it dangerous — because #23–#28 are genuine, `BASELINES.md` reads as internally consistent and nothing signals that #89 or #98 is not.

**Numbers are dropped rather than repointed or preserved.** A claim anchored to a tracker rots; a claim anchored to code does not, so `**Fixed (#230):**` becomes `**Fixed:**` followed by the file that fixed it. Where a real public issue does exist the reference stays — #23–#28, #45, #69, #87, #118 all verified against their titles.

## Twelve bad references in BASELINES.md — one more than the issue found

| ref | cited for | actually resolves to |
|---|---|---|
| **#20** | *"RFC #20 put the host wire on HTTP"* | "pnpm test -- \<filter\> does not filter" |
| **#87** | the Redis tier labelling | "Runtime features that no example demonstrates" |
| #89 ×6 | socket count, pool candidates, extrapolations | "Bring perf/ under lint and typecheck" |
| #90 | session tokens | "Collapse perf/aks and perf/app" |
| #95 | the pre-registered transport gate | PR "docs(counter): give the example a README" |
| #96 | the HMAC measurement | "Actor URLs still spend percent-escapes" |
| #98 ×2 | the tuned HTTP baseline | "bench: interleave the A/B" |
| #105 | the transport decision | PR "fix(wire): clean-URL grammar" |
| #132, #218, #230 ×2, #263, #284 | various | nothing (404) |

**#20 is the one worth flagging.** It sat under the load-bearing argument for why HTTP stays the default — the worst possible place for a reference that resolves to a test-filter bug.

## Two factual corrections in the same file

**The undici major.** The dispatcher table claimed 7.29 is *"the major Node currently bundles for the global `fetch`"*. It was measured on Node 24; the package's `engines` range is `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0`, and Node 22.22.0 ships undici **6.23.0** (verified locally). The section already warned in bold that the major matters while asserting one that does not hold across the supported range — the warning is now scoped accordingly.

**A fixed hazard written as a live one.** The "Also observed" TTL-pause split-brain — *"Single activation is not preserved across that window"* — is #45, and it is closed. A host now fences when it cannot prove its own membership, including when a beat merely *lands* past the TTL. The measurement stays as a record of the run that found it, explicitly labelled not-current. Per the issue, this nearly shipped into a public RFC as an unfixed-hazard non-goal.

Also: `benchmarks/README.md` said interpreting a 100-host run *"needs cluster-wide stats that do not exist yet"* — `clusterStats()` ships.

## Four cross-references broken by #114

My own regression: #114 cut the package README those sections lived in. `BASELINES.md`, `perf/aks/deploy/chart/values.yaml`, `docs/job-recipes.md` and `examples/counter/job-demo.mjs` now point at the docs site.

## The guard

`scripts/check-issue-refs.mjs` + a CI job (`pnpm verify:refs`). It enforces only the two failure modes that need no judgement:

1. `#N` above the repo's highest issue/PR number — stale by construction.
2. `#N` that 404s.

It deliberately does **not** guess whether a *resolvable* number is cited for the right thing; a check that guessed would be ignored. Cross-repo refs must be written `owner/repo#N` and are skipped.

Scoped to `benchmarks/`, `docs/`, and the root docs so it starts green — widen `DEFAULT_PATHS` as each remaining area is cleaned. Offline or without a token it degrades to a warning and exit 0 rather than passing silently (verified with an invalid token).

It earned its keep during review: it caught a stale `#245` in `AGENTS.md`, and an earlier version of its regex that required whitespace before the `#` found nine references where there were sixty — `(#245)` is the common form here.

## Out of scope, filed as #122

403 more occurrences across CHANGELOGs (225), `packages/` (156), `perf/` (14) and `.github/` (3) — 113 distinct numbers, 54 above the repo's highest. The changelog ones are a genuinely different question (they are records of what shipped, so rewriting them edits published history) and #122 lays out the options.

## Verification

- `pnpm verify:refs` — all 15 refs in the guarded paths resolve.
- Every remaining ref in `benchmarks/` re-resolved by hand against its surrounding claim, not just for existence.
- `pnpm typecheck` clean; `pnpm lint` clean (one pre-existing warning in `cluster/load-policy.ts`, untouched).
- `pnpm test`: **1474 passed**, 130 skipped, no type errors.

No behaviour change — comments, docs, one new script and one CI job.

items.title: fix(ci): build dist before running benchmarks
items.body:
The Benchmarks workflow crashed on the v1.5.0 release ([run 31267507913](https://github.com/jeremydaly/lambda-api/actions/runs/31267507913)):

```
Error: Cannot find module '/home/runner/work/lambda-api/lambda-api/dist/cjs/index.js'.
Please verify that the package.json has a valid "main" entry
    at Object.<anonymous> (benchmarks/frameworks/lambda-api.js:10:19)
```

## Root cause

`benchmarks/frameworks/lambda-api.js` loads the library from the working tree with `require('../../')`, which resolves through the root package's `main`. #326 changed `main` from `index.js` to `./dist/cjs/index.js`, so the adapter now requires a build — but the workflow only ran `npm ci` inside `benchmarks/`, never installing or building the root package.

The benchmark suite (#327) merged before the dual build (#326), and benchmarks only run on `release: published`, so v1.5.0 was the first time the two met. The `baseline` framework has no lambda-api dependency and completed fine, which is why the log shows 10 green scenarios before the crash.

## Fixes

**1. Build `dist/` before benchmarking.** Adds a root `npm ci --ignore-scripts` + `npm run build` ahead of the benchmark install, matching how `release.yml` sequences the same steps.

**2. Honor `LAMBDA_API_VERSION` in the adapter.** Surfaced while verifying the first fix. `run.js:65` already read the env var, but only for the run metadata that renders the caption — the per-framework table rows use each adapter's own `version` field, and lambda-api's read `package.json` directly. Since that ships a `0.0.0-development` placeholder until publish time, every table row would have rendered as:

```
| lambda-api `0.0.0-development` | 298,049 | ...
```

while the caption directly above it correctly said `lambda-api v1.5.0`. That would have been committed straight into the README by the workflow's final step. The adapter now uses the same `LAMBDA_API_VERSION || pkg.version` precedence as `run.js`.

## Verification

Reproduced locally by deleting `dist/` — same `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at the same adapter line; loads cleanly after `npm run build`.

Ran the exact workflow command end-to-end (`node run.js --md results/RESULTS.md --json results/raw.json --update-readme` with `LAMBDA_API_VERSION=1.5.0`). All 6 frameworks × 10 scenarios complete, and both the caption and every table row now read `1.5.0`. Generated results were reverted out of this branch — the committed numbers should come from the runner, not my laptop.

The subsequent `Format README` step pins `prettier@2`, which matches the repo's `^2.3.2` devDependency, so no version skew there.

## Note

The v1.5.0 README still has stale benchmark numbers, since the workflow never reached its commit step. Once this merges, re-running the workflow via `workflow_dispatch` with version `1.5.0` will refresh it.

items.title: feat(bench): weekly head-to-head benchmark with generated badges
items.body:
## Summary

- Replaces the hand-typed Performance table with **generated badges** served from GitHub Pages. The README markup is frozen — only URLs — so weekly numbers refresh with **zero commits to main** and zero load on eslint.interlace.tools.
- Adds **ILB-Headline**: 4 stacks (Interlace on ESLint, Interlace on oxlint, the community stack, stock oxlint) across two real repos — nestjs (Node) and shadcn-ui (frontend).
- Adds **job-level matchups**: the comparison unit is a *capability*, not a package, with specific rules named on both sides.
- Adds `weekly-benchmark.yml` (Mon 09:00 UTC): build → verify matchups → bench both repos → gate → Supabase → badges → Pages.
- Retargets two growth CTAs to the ecosystem site, locked by a test.

## Why the old table had to go

It claimed a **51% oxlint cache benefit** where its own cited scorecard says **1%** — a different conclusion, not a rounding error. Its numbers were also three months stale.

Root cause: a partial flagship snapshot (1 of 10 rules) landed in `results/`, the loader silently fell back to an older complete one, and the bench *looked* run while publishing stale numbers. Every command in that pipeline exited 0. `scripts/verify-weekly-benchmark.ts` now fails on exactly that.

## Apples-to-apples

Whole-plugin comparison misleads in both directions — SonarJS ships 279 rules (mostly code smells), `no-unsanitized` ships 2 (excellent ones). So each row names the specific rules on both sides, scoped to **security + module integrity only**.

Competitors are named, versioned, and linked: `eslint-plugin-security`, `sonarjs`, `@microsoft/eslint-plugin-sdl`, `no-unsanitized`, `security-node`, `no-secrets`, `regexp`, `import`.

**15 of 17 contested jobs are faster.** The 2 losses (path traversal, timing-attack comparison) stay in the table, and each matchup carries a note where the competitor is genuinely better.

## Honesty rails — each earned by a bug caught while building this

| Rail | The bug it caught |
| :--- | :--- |
| File-set parity asserted | oxlint linted 1714 files while ESLint linted 1 — parity still reported YES |
| `MIN_FILES = 50` | a 1-file root glob passed as a valid benchmark |
| Only `ruleId` findings counted | parse errors made every job report an identical ~689 findings |
| Failures recorded, not dropped | a 0-file run parsed as the fastest possible bar |
| Snapshot named `<date>-<repo>` | the second repo silently destroyed the first's results |
| Stock oxlint excluded from "fastest" | different rule scope — no secrets/injection/CSP analysis |

## `verify-matchups.ts` caught 18 fabricated rule IDs

While authoring the matchup table, **18 of 54 rule IDs did not exist** — plausible names written from memory rather than read from the plugins (`secure-coding/no-eval-usage` vs the real `browser-security/no-eval`). A public comparison citing non-existent rules is checkable, and someone would have checked.

It now runs **before every benchmark** and as a **vitest lock**, so a renamed rule fails the PR rather than the Monday job.

## Test plan

- [x] `verify-matchups.ts` — 99 rule references across 18 matchups, all verified
- [x] `benchmark-integrity-lock.test.ts` — 107 tests; **mutation-tested**: renaming a rule makes it fail, then restored
- [x] `growth-conversion-lock.test.ts` — 24 pass, CTA URLs locked
- [x] Both locks together: **131 tests pass** against this branch's README
- [x] `typecheck:scripts` + `typecheck:benchmarks` clean
- [x] Workflow YAML validated (caught and fixed a block-scalar parse error)
- [x] End-to-end local run on an isolated shallow clone

## Before merging

**Badge URLs 404 until the workflow runs once.** GitHub Pages is enabled (`build_type: workflow`) but nothing has deployed. `workflow_dispatch` cannot target a branch until the workflow exists on the default branch — so the sequence is: **merge this → run `weekly-benchmark.yml` manually → badges resolve.** There is a short window where the README shows broken images; running the workflow immediately after merge closes it.

Requires the Supabase migration `20260809000000_benchmark_runs.sql` (agents repo). Without it the publish step fails non-fatally and badges still render from the local snapshot.

items.title: fix(ci): Align benchmark ids with the pinned harness
items.body:
Follow-up to #339. With the install fixed, the benchmark job now gets far enough to fail at the *next* step.

### What

Renames three benchmark ids to match what js-framework-benchmark actually emits, in all four places that must agree.

| Ours (stale) | Pinned harness |
| --- | --- |
| `03_update10th1k` | `03_update10th1k_x16` |
| `09_clear1k` | `09_clear1k_x8` |
| `25_clear-memory` | `25_run-clear-memory` |

### Why

```
❌ Missing benchmark data:
  - Missing CI result for duration benchmark: 03_update10th1k (Update every 10th row ×16)
  - Missing CI result for duration benchmark: 09_clear1k (Clear 1,000 rows ×8)
  - Missing CI result for memory benchmark: 25_clear-memory (Clear memory)
```

Our **labels** already said "×16" and "×8" — only the **ids** were left behind, which is the signature of a partial rename that went unnoticed because the job had been dying earlier at `npm ci`.

I confirmed the correct names against `webdriver-ts/src/benchmarksCommon.ts` at the pinned commit rather than inferring them from the error message, and cross-checked that all 12 ids the README script expects now exist in the harness.

**All four files have to move together.** The README script looks up the CI result *and* the Blazor reference by the same key, so renaming the workflow and scripts without `blazor-baseline.json` would just trade `Missing CI result` for `Missing Blazor baseline`. The Blazor measurements themselves are unchanged — only their keys move, and the baseline's `notes` field now records that.

### One thing worth knowing

Two of the stale ids (`03_update10th1k`, `09_clear1k`) happened to **prefix-match** and ran anyway, writing results under the full name — which is why only the README step noticed. `25_clear-memory` matched nothing, and the runner **exited cleanly having measured nothing**:

```
> node dist/benchmarkRunner.js --headless --framework keyed/abies --benchmark 25_clear-memory
  benchmark: [ '25_clear-memory' ],
```

No error, no result. An unrecognised benchmark id is silent, so a typo here costs a metric rather than a red build.

### On the baseline

Re-baselining turned out to be unnecessary — **it already self-healed.** Once #339 let the job run, main's push run reported `✅ No regressions detected` and published a fresh baseline to `gh-pages` (`7a0feb6`). The stale March numbers I flagged were an artifact of the workflow's refresh step never being reached while the install was broken.

### Testing

- All four files validate: JSON parses, YAML parses, both Python scripts compile.
- Cross-checked the script's 12 expected ids against the pinned harness's definitions — **none missing**.
- This PR touches `benchmark.yml`, which is in the workflow's own `e2e-scripts` filter, so it triggers a **real benchmark run** and is verified end-to-end by its own CI.

items.title: bench: fix W1/W2/W4 output mismatches and implement real W5
items.body:
## Summary

Stage B / W5 measurements on the v0.2.0-niche / v0.3.0-negative tag were comparing **different programs** on BT-IS and SCALAR, so the instruction ratios did not measure the architectures on equivalent work. This PR rewrites all four workloads so BT-IS and SCALAR produce identical output on a fair comparison, then implements the canonicalization flagship that PLAN_6_STEPS_STATUS.md Step 3 called for but was never actually run.

## Honesty gate

`benchmarks/stage_b_word.py` and the new `benchmarks/stage_b_w5.py` **assert output equality** before reporting any instruction-count ratio. If BT-IS and SCALAR don't produce the same output, the script exits non-zero and prints FAIL. The old version of `stage_b_word.py` counted ops without checking outputs.

## Workload results (after fix)

| Workload                | BT-IS | SCALAR | ratio | output match |
|-------------------------|------:|-------:|------:|:------------:|
| W1 rotations            |     9 |     14 | 1.56x |   yes        |
| W2 voxel_count (3 alive) |   34 |     52 | 1.53x |   yes        |
| W4 cubeadd_loop (10x)   |    32 |     22 | 0.69x |   yes        |
| W5 48 O_h inner loop    |   281 |    384 | 1.37x |   yes        |

Pre-correction numbers in `docs/STAGE_B_RESULTS.md` and `docs/STAGE_W5_RESULTS.md` (1.40x, 0.85x, 1.47x, 0.67x) were on mismatched programs. The honest numbers above are different: BT-IS wins on three workloads, loses on one.

## Why W4 changed sign

The previous W4 measured different recurrences:
- BT-IS: `C := C + mem[C]` (the cube_add primitive as defined). After iter 0, C's address changed so `mem[C]` was empty and subsequent iterations were no-ops.
- SCALAR: `C0 := C0 + C0` (always real work).

This rewrite makes BT-IS do `C := C + C` directly using D0 to hold the running operand and refreshing it after each `cube_add`. The honest ratio is 22/32 = 0.69x: BT-IS is **slower** on the pure cube-add primitive when both compute the same recurrence. The 1.47x headline was an artifact of comparing different programs.

## W5 was a 7-term composition, not canonicalization

The previous `programs/w5_compose.btis` and `benchmarks/w5_scalar.py` claimed to test the canonicalization flagship ("apply all 48 O_h elements, pick the lex-minimum"). They actually tested a single 7-term composition followed by one apply. The PLAN-recommended canonicalization experiment was never run.

This PR implements the **inner loop of canonicalization** on a single cube:
- Generate the 48 O_h permutations (24 proper + 24 improper).
- Verify group axioms: bijectivity, closure over all 2304 pairs, negation maps proper to improper.
- For each permutation, factor it into a minimum-length sequence of named BT-IS rotor ops (BFS; max factor length: 3).
- Emit the BT-IS program and a SCALAR equivalent.
- Assert both produce the same 48-output orbit (each of 6 axial states x 8).

W5 honest result: **BT-IS 1.37x faster** on setup cost. BT-IS loads a permutation into R0 in 0-3 named `rot_*_r` / `reflect_*_r` / `neg_r` instructions, then `apply_r 0`. SCALAR has no cube-copy primitive, so it must rebuild the input cube from scratch each iteration using 3 LOAD_IMM + 3 CGET = 6 ops. Both architectures pay 1 op for the apply itself.

## What this does NOT prove

- The original 48x canonicalization claim was for an `apply_r_to_mem` opcode that operates on a 27-cell pattern. That opcode does not exist in the current ISA. The current `apply_r` is one permutation applied to one cube, so the 27x outer factor cancels out. The 1.37x win is the setup cost only.
- The full W1/W2/W4/W5 work does not establish a general BT-IS advantage; it's mixed (3 wins, 1 loss on a fair comparison).
- The new honest ratios supersede the v0.2.0-niche and v0.3.0-negative numbers in `docs/RESULTS.md` and `VERDICT.md`. A follow-up commit will update those documents.

## Files added

- `benchmarks/stage_b_w5.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/oh.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/verify.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/factor.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/factor_sequences.json`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/gen_w5_btis.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/oh_perms.json`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/w5_scalar.py`
- `programs/w5_canon.btis`

## Files modified

- `benchmarks/scalar_vm_word.py` (add REFLECT_X/Y/Z constants)
- `benchmarks/stage_b_word.py` (output-equality gate)
- `benchmarks/w1_word_scalar.py` (mirror BT-IS sequence)
- `benchmarks/w2_word_scalar.py` (fix register bug, 3-alive pattern)
- `programs/w4_cubeadd.btis` (rewrite for C := C + C)
- `programs/w2_voxel_count.btis` (rewrite to match SCALAR)
- `docs/STAGE_W5_RESULTS.md` (rewrite to describe the real 48 O_h workload)

## How to verify

```bash
git checkout v0.3.1-fixes
python3 benchmarks/stage_b_word.py
python3 benchmarks/stage_b_w5.py
```

Both should exit 0 with all four workloads reporting OK and a ratio column.

## Out of scope for this PR

The original review surfaced other issues that are not addressed here:
- Stage A programs (`gcd.btis`, `life3d_step.btis`, `sort3x3x3.btis` are still stubs)
- Turing-completeness proof (assumes unbounded memory that does not exist)
- VM/assembler bugs (silent operand default, register-mask bounds check, BR_AXIS unreachable, undo_all incomplete)
- Verilog core (most opcodes are TODO stubs; area/timing claims are projections, not measurements)
- Documentation drift (CHANGELOG, README, prompts reference stale numbers and counts)

These should be addressed in separate PRs.

items.body:
## What problem are you trying to solve?

`docs/current/AEGIS_AGENTIC_BENCHMARK_BASELINE.md` states four run-shape values
that contradict the matrix fixture the same section names as their owner.

The section opens with:

> The matrix is the only exact run-shape owner. It defines these profiles:

…and then restates the profile table. Four of those restated numbers are stale
— each one is exactly half of the value currently in
`tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json`:

| Value | Baseline doc (lines 199-201, 204) | Matrix fixture (lines 134-191) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `development-pilot` wall budget | 600 seconds | **1200** |
| `standard-held-out` wall budget | 3600 seconds | **7200** |
| `extended-held-out` wall budget | 9000 seconds | **18000** |
| per-attempt timeout | 480 seconds | **960** |

Root cause is traceable to a single commit. `c38a24a6`
(`perf: double agentic benchmark budgets for slow providers`, shipped in
v2.6.9) changed four files:

```
tests/e2e/agentic-benchmark-check.sh
tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json
tests/helpers/test_run_agentic_benchmark.py
tests/helpers/validate_agentic_benchmark_matrix.py
```

The v2.6.9 release note for that change says the three profile definitions
("check 脚本内嵌、校验脚本、fixture 矩阵") were kept in sync. The prose baseline
is a fourth place that also restates those values, and it was not updated.

Concrete impact: the baseline docs are the documented authority read order for
non-trivial work (`AGENTS.md` → `docs/current/README.md` → task-relevant
`docs/current/*.md`). An agent or contributor sizing a benchmark run from this
table plans against half the real ceiling — for `extended-held-out`, 9000s
instead of 18000s. Nothing in the suite compares the prose table against the
matrix, so this drift is silent: the three profile assertions in
`agentic-benchmark-check.sh` pass identically before and after this change
(verified below), because they assert profile presence and policy wording, not
the numeric values.

## What does this PR change?

Updates four stale numbers in `docs/current/AEGIS_AGENTIC_BENCHMARK_BASELINE.md`
to match `tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json`. Documentation only
— no code, fixture, test, or behavior change.

## Is this change appropriate for the core library?

Yes. It corrects a `docs/current/` authority document that ships with the
method pack and is part of the documented read order for every user, on every
project type. It is not project-specific, team-specific, or tool-specific, and
it introduces no third-party service or integration.

## What alternatives did you consider?

1. **Remove the numbers from the prose table entirely**, leaving the matrix as
   the sole carrier. Rejected: the section's stated purpose is to describe what
   the matrix defines, and the surrounding prose depends on those figures
   (the wall-clock budget paragraph immediately after explains what the ceiling
   covers). Deleting the table also removes useful reference material, and that
   editorial call belongs to the maintainer, not to an outside contributor.
2. **Extend the automated checks so the prose table is compared against the
   matrix**, which would prevent the next recurrence rather than fixing this
   instance. Rejected *for this PR* because it is a separate, unrelated change
   to the test suite and would bundle two changes into one PR. I am happy to
   open it separately if you want it.
3. **Open an issue instead of a PR.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks for issue-first on
   non-trivial changes; a four-number correction with a traceable root cause is
   trivial enough that a diff is faster to review than a description. Happy to
   convert to an issue if you prefer that ordering.

## Does this PR contain multiple unrelated changes?

No. One file, four lines, one concern: aligning stale restated values with the
fixture that owns them.

## Existing PRs
- [x] I have reviewed all open AND closed PRs for duplicates or prior art
- Related PRs: none found — at the time of writing this repository has no open
  PRs, and no closed-unmerged PRs; the only merged PRs are the maintainer's own.

## Environment tested

| Harness (e.g. Claude Code, Cursor) | Harness version | Model | Model version/ID |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------|-------|------------------|
| Claude Code (used to prepare and verify this change) | 2.1.221 | Claude Opus 5 | `claude-opus-5[1m]` |

Verification commands were run on macOS 26.6 (Darwin 25.6.0), bash 5.x,
Python 3.14.6, against `main` at `fe34c3c` (v2.6.9).

## Evaluation

This is a documentation value correction with no behavior surface, so
before/after eval sessions are not the applicable instrument — there is no
agent behavior to measure, and I did not run any. What I did instead was verify
correctness of the values and prove the change is regression-free against a
stashed baseline:

**1. Value correctness.** Each new number read directly out of
`tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json`
(`wallClockBudgetSeconds` = 1200 / 7200 / 18000, `perAttemptTimeoutSeconds`
= 960 on all three profiles), cross-checked against the v2.6.9 release note and
against commit `c38a24a6`.

**2. Scope check — nothing else drifted.** Every other value in the table was
compared to the fixture and matches: repetitions 1/1/3, valid target 2/40/120,
attempt ceiling 2/44/132, workers 2/8/8, preflight 30s, max workers 12. Those
are left untouched.

**3. Repo-wide sweep for other stale copies.** Grepped the whole tree for the
old values; the only occurrences outside this file are in `RELEASE-NOTES.md`,
where they are historical `600→1200` change records and must stay.

**4. Before/after regression proof** (change stashed, re-run, unstashed):

| --- | --- | --- |
| `tests/e2e/agentic-benchmark-check.sh` | 55 pass, 0 fail, exit 1 | 55 pass, 0 fail, exit 1 |

items.title: bench+docs: the BENCH_SPEC rows the suite never ran, and the README shape §9 prescribes
items.body:
Two related pieces of spec conformance: the benchmark suite measured 4 of
BENCH_SPEC's 10 required rows, and the README had drifted from the shape
CORELIB_PLAN §9 fixes for every corelib. The library itself is untouched — no
file under `src/` changes.

## `bench`: the six missing rows

Each of the six is the only place in the suite that reaches a whole path:
`blob 1MB` (one-shot / streaming / decode) is the only workload that reaches
CORELIB_PLAN §5.1's divisible-run path, and `composite` (encode / decode /
skip-all) the only one touching a wrapper array, non-ASCII UTF-8, depth-3
nesting, a field the encoder must omit, or a two-byte field header.

Both datasets are built exactly as BENCH_SPEC states them — 1,000,005-byte
one-shot buffer sized by hand, 4096-byte streaming buffer with a sink that
consumes and discards, 4096-byte decode chunks, no pass-through permission — and
`bench/run_callgrind.sh` gains all ten workloads in spec row order.

Three checks the numbers now have to pass:

- the blob parity size (1,000,005) is asserted one-shot **and** over the sink's
  byte count, and a mismatch aborts instead of printing a table;
- both decodes are replayed outside the timed loop and compared against the
  source, so a silently-skipping decoder cannot post a fast row;
- the single-shot diagnostic line carries an FNV-1a of the encoded message, and
  C and C++ agree on it (`5e9de7ec`, 956 bytes) — which is what makes the
  C-vs-C++ instruction table mean anything.

The four pre-existing rows measure identically at four workloads and at ten
(966 / 2109 / 125 999 / 300 432), so no `flatten` on the toggle points is needed
here.

**What the new rows say.** The one-shot-to-streaming delta is 4,657 Ir — 0.05 %,
not the double-digit fraction BENCH_SPEC anticipates. `_write_fixlen` pushes
every payload byte through `_push_byte`, so the copy costs ~10 Ir/byte encoding
and ~25 decoding and the flush machinery vanishes next to it. That is a property
of the corelib, not of the bench, and is left alone in this PR.

## README: §9 shape and stale facts

Three §9 violations fixed — the two-corelib comparison demoted to the final
subsection of Benchmarks (§9.8), `Feature flags` and `Sequence framing` demoted
under Usage (they were invented top-level sections), and the CI badge added to
the §9.2 block. Anchors are unchanged, so every internal link still resolves.
§9.6's required pass-through statement was missing and is now in Memory handling.

Feature flags: `SOFAB_BUILD_TESTS` and `SOFAB_INSTALL` were undocumented; the
table presented every switch as a macro to define, which is exactly the form
`utils/ci/build-config.sh` exists to warn about; and
`SOFAB_DISABLE_LAZY_SEQ_SUPPORT` is the one switch with **no CMake option**, so
`-D…=ON` is silently ignored and the build comes out unreduced while looking
configured. That last one is documented here as a warning — adding the missing
option is a build-system change and belongs in its own PR.

Footprint gains a per-switch table (generated by the same `tools/footprint.sh`,
extended to measure it). Notable: the deltas do not add up, because the switches
overlap, and `SOFAB_OBJECT_DESCR_PROFILE=SMALL` makes the library **20 B
bigger** — the profile sizes the descriptor tables in the consumer's `.rodata`,
while narrower members cost the library a few widening instructions.

Re-measuring corrected three stale numbers: the ARMv7-m Full row and the four
strict-UTF-8 rows were one rounding step low, "ARMv6-m returns to 3326 B" is
3545 B, and the hold-back costs **+6 Ir/op** on `encode: typical message`, not
+56 — the old reading predates `9f124b1` collapsing the per-type dispatch.

The `corelib-cpp` comparison was wrong in three rows after that port's recent
work: it no longer hands back zero-copy `string_view`s, it now ships the same
three heap-free field types, and it has `MessageSeq` (which this port
deliberately dropped). The Ir/op table is re-measured and extended to all ten
rows now that both ports run them. Nine go to `corelib-cpp` by 1.4×–10×;
`encode: blob 1MB streaming` goes the other way by **1.3×**, because its `memcpy`
branch only holds while the run fits the buffer — this core has no fast path to
fall out of.

## Verification

- `bench_c`, `bench_cpp`, `perf_c`, `perf_cpp` build warning-free at
  `-Wall -Wextra`; all four run, `perf` still reports 170 bytes.
- Full `run_callgrind.sh` produces all ten rows for both languages.
- `bench_c` also builds and produces byte-identical composite output with
  `SOFAB_DISABLE_LAZY_SEQ_SUPPORT`.
- `tools/footprint.sh` runs end to end: 16 configuration builds + 12 switch
  builds across all four cross toolchains.
- **Not run:** the CTest suite. Nothing under `src/` is touched, so the library
  and its tests are unaffected; CI covers it.

items.title: Add the browser path, fix two unusable dependency floors, and benchmark the whole item
items.body:
Validated against Frostwork main. Four commits, each reviewable on its own.

## Two dependency floors that don't install

- **`scrapy-poet>=0.24` → `>=0.26`.** `demo/settings.py` wires everything through
  `ADDONS = {"scrapy_poet.Addon": 300}`, and `Addon` first appears in 0.26.0. On 0.24/0.25 every crawl dies
  at startup: `NameError: Module 'scrapy_poet' doesn't define any object named 'Addon'`.
- **`scrapy>=2.11` → `>=2.14`.** The code does run on 2.11.2, but Scrapy below 2.14 doesn't cap Twisted,
  and Twisted ≥ 25.5 removed `_setAcceptableProtocols` — so a fresh resolve can't load a download handler
  at all.
- Drops `REQUEST_FINGERPRINTER_IMPLEMENTATION`, which no longer exists in Scrapy.

## The browser path (`scrapy crawl commerce_browser`)

`FrostBrowserPage` had no coverage here. The schema now lives on `ProductFields(FrostFields)` and is bound
to both response contracts, so the direct and browser paths genuinely share it instead of keeping two
copies in step. The storefront serves `#delivery` empty and hydrates it client-side, so the browser path
reaches two fields the direct path cannot while every other field stays byte-identical.

`browser` is an optional extra — `uv sync && uv run pytest` still works with no browser installed (13 pass,
1 skip).

**Reviewer note:** the `BrowserResponseProvider` here is demo-only. On Zyte API, `ZyteApiProvider` already
provides `BrowserResponse`, so a `FrostBrowserPage` needs no wiring — this demo writes one because it runs
without an API key, on scrapy-playwright. The README says so, so nobody copies it into a Zyte project that
doesn't need it.

## The benchmark measured less than the README claimed

`bench.py` timed the 11 flat selectors and none of the six `Many`/`One` collections, while the README
claimed every field rides the one scan. It now times both and asserts parity over every group row. The
correction makes Frostwork look better — the collections are where a one-pass engine wins most:

| | Parsel | Frostwork | |
|---|---|---|---|
| flat fields only (11 selectors) | ~12.7 ms/page | ~1.00 ms/page | ~13× |
| whole item (+6 groups) | ~20.6 ms/page | ~1.15 ms/page | **~18×** |

Going from 11 selectors to the whole item costs Frostwork +0.15 ms and Parsel +8 ms. The old README numbers
were stale in the other direction; they're replaced with measured ones.

## Verification

- 14 Scrapy wirings, Scrapy 2.11–2.17, Python 3.12–3.14 — **0 item divergences**
- 15 encoding shapes vs Parsel — **0 divergences**
- Browser vs direct — 29/29 hydrated, **0 divergences** on every wire-visible field
- Whole-item parity vs Parsel, 40 × ~555 KB pages, flat columns and every group row — **0 mismatches**
- Demo suite 14 passed; zero deprecation warnings anywhere

`docs/VALIDATION-2026-08-05.md` has the full matrix and the library feedback, including two suggestions
worth upstreaming.

items.title: bench(public): regenerate the Node/Bun baseline at v0.5.1335 and restore the README markers
items.body:
Unblocks the public-baseline gate. `lint` has been red on `main` and on every open PR, for **two independent reasons** — I only knew about one of them until the run actually completed.

## 1. The artifact was stale — and the gate was right

`source_fingerprint` covers `Cargo.toml`, and #7302 changed `panic = "unwind"` → `panic = "abort"` in both the `release` and `dist` profiles. That is a real, benchmark-relevant change, so the demand for a regeneration was correct rather than a fingerprinting artifact. (My first hypothesis was that the version bump invalidated it on every merge; that is already normalised by `_CARGO_VERSION_RE`, so it was wrong.)

Regenerated on the pinned quiet M1 Max — the host the artifact's own `host.cpu` names — with pinned `node v22.23.1` / `bun 1.3.14` / `zig 0.15.2`, all five `wait_for_quiet` gates passed, at `2ba59501b` (v0.5.1335). All five components present, `validate_public` passes.

## 2. `public_baseline.py check` could never pass

#6736 rewrote `README.md` as a marketing landing page and deleted the `<!-- public-node-bun:start -->` / `<!-- public-node-bun:end -->` markers, replacing the generated block with a hand-maintained table. `_replace_block` therefore raised `README generated markers are missing` on **every** invocation, independent of the artifact. No amount of regenerating would have fixed it.

That is worth naming as a pattern rather than a typo: a gate whose subject was deleted still runs, still reports, and can never go green — so it stops being a gate and becomes a permanent reason to bypass. Same family as #7582.

The markers are restored **under the sentence that promises them** — *"We publish everything, including the workloads where V8's JIT still beats us — no cherry-picked table can survive an open harness"* — inside a collapsed `<details>`, so the landing page keeps the shape #6736 deliberately chose while the published numbers are once again **derived from the artifact** instead of hand-maintained. The generated table is what makes that sentence true: it carries `prime_sieve` 30 ms vs 6, and `matrix_multiply` 87 ms vs 34, as losses.

`python3 benchmarks/public_baseline.py check` now exits **0**.

## What the run measured

Two results worth surfacing, both with output verified against the Bun reference 20/20:

- **`image_convolution` 302.5 ms** — 3.1× faster than bun (947.2), faster than **Rust** (429.8), within 8% of Zig (279.8).
- **`json_pipeline` at 100 records: 77.0 ms** — ahead of bun (90.8) and node (128.1), within 5% of Rust and Zig, at **8.5 MB RSS against bun's 30.3**.

And one that is not good, filed as **#7592**: the same JSON workload at **500,000 records is 60,358 ms against bun's 618 ms — 97.6×**. It is a scaling cliff rather than a constant factor (Perry grows 784× across the fixture increase where bun grows 6.8×, Rust 8.9×, Zig 12.0×). Correct output, 20/20 — purely performance.

That row is now published by this PR, which is the point of the mechanism.

## Note for follow-up

`README.md`'s hand-written table cites `honest_bench/REPORT.md` for its JSON row and shows the 100-record variant; the same report's 500k variant is the 97.6× row above. Its absolute numbers are also stale — the JSON row reads 39 ms where today measures 77 ms, though bun (51 → 90.8) and Rust (34 → 73.4) moved by the same factor, so that is measurement conditions rather than a Perry regression, and the relative ordering holds. Reconciling that table is a product decision about the landing page and is left to the owner; this PR does not touch it.

  ```yaml
  %TAG ! !foo
  ---
  bar
  ```
- A **`%YAML` directive with a higher major version** (e.g. `%YAML 2.0`) used to parse silently; it's now rejected, per [YAML 1.2.2 §6.8.1](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#681-yaml-directives). A higher *minor* (`1.3`) and `%YAML 1.1`/`1.2` are unaffected.
- Both match `js-yaml`; the yaml-test-suite score is unchanged (364/373). Recorded in README's "Decisions and deviations" as intentional strictness over the lenient `yaml` library.

**2. Cap the key-intern cache to bound peak memory** — Closes #136.
- `keyCache` had no size limit (its sibling caches do), so an all-distinct-key document (e.g. a UUID/hostname/timestamp lookup table) grew it unbounded. It's now capped by **cumulative key size (4 MB default)**, and the cap is exposed as an opt-in `optimizations.keyCacheMaxKb` on `parse`/`parseAll`. Parsed output is byte-for-byte unchanged; the `./yaml`/`./js-yaml` compat shims are untouched.

**3. Show the README benchmark table as ratios** — Closes #137.
- The hero table's absolute ms/MB drift with the benchmark box (the old numbers were stale, but the apparent "regression" was a CI-runner baseline shift — `JSON.parse`'s own numbers moved the same way, not a lightning-yaml regression). It now shows **ratios to `JSON.parse`** — parse ~2.1×, peak-RSS ~1.4× for lightning-yaml — which don't swing with the machine, sourced from the newest [`benchmark-data`](https://github.com/jbsiddall/lightning-yaml/tree/benchmark-data) run (commit `4ca6140`, 2026-07-23) with a visible provenance line. The stale "3–5× faster" speed claim was corrected too.

## Correctness gate

- [x] `pnpm typecheck` · `pnpm test` (59/59)
- [x] `pnpm test:unit` (440/440, incl. new directive + key-cache tests) · `pnpm test:stringify` (218/218)
- [x] `pnpm test:suite` — **364/373 (97.6%), unchanged** · `pnpm test:compat` — unchanged
- [x] `pnpm bench:self` — no regression (the key-cache byte-counter is O(1)/key; directive checks are cold-path)

## Code review

- [x] `/code-review` passed — **all eight reviewers approved at commit `fe6999cb87da`**. Pushing new commits invalidates this: re-run `/code-review` and update the hash until all reviewers approve the new HEAD.

Deferred non-blocking notes (would reset the unanimous sign-off for cosmetic gain): the `parse`/`parseAll` per-call option apply/restore is duplicated (tracked in #141), and a `dumpKeyCache` comment still says "mirror" though the two caps now use different strategies — both can ride the #141 cleanup.

## Changeset

- [x] Two changesets, both **minor** for `lightning-yaml`: `reject-malformed-directives` (the two new directive errors) and `cap-key-cache-memory` (adds the public `keyCacheMaxKb` option). The README change is docs-only.

## Correctness note

The two directive changes are the only parse-behavior changes, both spec-backed:
- Duplicate `%TAG` per handle — [§6.8.2](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#682-tag-directives): "It is an error to specify more than one `TAG` directive for the same handle in the same document." (`js-yaml` throws; the `yaml` oracle accepts, but per CLAUDE.md the spec adjudicates over the oracle — recorded as a sanctioned strictness in README.)
- Higher-major `%YAML` — [§6.8.1](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#681-yaml-directives): a higher major version "should be rejected with an appropriate error message." Only `major ≠ 1` is rejected.

The key-cache cap and README rework change no parse/dump behavior.

  for 6 languages and "15" for C#/Java/Scala, while prose ~25 lines later
  claimed "all 18 patterns across 9 languages." Re-derived every number from
  `feature-manifest.json` and cross-checked with direct source inspection
  rather than trusting either the old README or the manifest blindly.
- Rewrote the 4 bare "Nx faster than Python" performance claims (the "Key
  Insight" callout plus the Go/Rust/Zig code-sample comments) to name what
  they measure — framework/transport overhead, not general app performance —
  matching the dated-methodology caveat COMPATIBILITY.md already carries for
  the same numbers.
- Deleted the stale `docs/parity/FEATURE_MATRIX.md` (dated 2026-03-16,
  describes "all 6 Agenkit language implementations"; repo now has 9).
  Confirmed nothing reads it as an input before deleting — it's purely
  generated output of `scripts/parity/matrix_generator.py`.

## Verification (re-runnable)

**Pattern counts** — regenerated the manifest fresh and diffed against the
checked-in copy (only `generated_at` changed, confirming the data itself
isn't stale):

```
uv run python scripts/parity/feature_scanner.py
uv run python -c "import json; d=json.load(open('feature-manifest.json')); [print(l, len(v['patterns'])) for l,v in d['languages'].items()]"
-> python 24, go 17, typescript 17, rust 15, cpp 18, zig 13, csharp 15, java 15, scala 15
```

Cross-checked with direct source inspection (not just class counts) that
Python/Go/TypeScript/Rust/C++/Zig genuinely have all 18 named patterns —
e.g. `find agenkit-rust/src -iname "*sequential*" -o -iname "*parallel*"` etc.
for each of the 18 pattern names. The class-count differences within those
six are architectural (Python ships config/streaming variants like
`ConversationalAgentConfig`; C++ has `ReactAgent`/`ReasoningAgent` as
duplicate names for `ReActAgent`/`ReasoningWithToolsAgent`), not missing
patterns.

For C#/Java/Scala's "15," found two things while reconciling it against
reality:
1. **A scanner bug** (not a code gap): `scripts/parity/scanners/{csharp,java,scala}_scanner.py`
   only walk each language's `Patterns/` directory, but all three languages
   implement `SequentialAgent`/`ParallelAgent` under a sibling `Composition/`
   directory the scanner never visits. Verified by direct grep, e.g.
   `grep -n "public class SequentialAgent" agenkit-cs/src/Agenkit/Composition/SequentialAgent.cs`
   (and the Java/Scala equivalents) all hit — so the manifest's 15 undercounts
   by 2; the real number is 17 of 18.
2. **A real gap**: none of the three implement `AgentsAsTools`. Verified:
   `grep -rl AgentTool agenkit-cs agenkit-java agenkit-scala` finds nothing,
   vs. `agenkit/patterns/agents_as_tools.py` (and Go/TS/Rust/C++/Zig
   equivalents) in the other six.

The README now states this precisely: 6 languages at 18/18, C#/Java/Scala at
17/18 (missing `AgentsAsTools`) — in the table, the table caption, and the
"Project Status" bullet, so none of them contradict each other anymore.
Filed #913 for the longer-term fix (replacing this class-count model with
spec-conformance against `specs/patterns/*.yaml`); linked inline in the
README rather than building it here.

**Performance claims** — confirmed the exact multipliers and their dated
methodology:
```
grep -n "18.5x faster" benchmarks/BASELINES.md
-> Go HTTP: ... 18.5x faster than Python (0.055ms vs 1.02ms), dated 2025-11-11
grep -n "Performance Characteristics" -A20 COMPATIBILITY.md
-> already states these figures are from Nov 2025 against Python 3.14.0 /
   Go 1.21-1.22 on Apple Silicon, and toolchain versions have since moved
```
Reworded each README occurrence to match that same framing (e.g. "up to 18x
lower framework/transport overhead in our benchmarks" instead of "18x better
performance") and added a short caveat to the README's own Performance
section that cross-links `COMPATIBILITY.md#performance-characteristics`
instead of duplicating/contradicting it.

**FEATURE_MATRIX.md deletion** — confirmed nothing depends on it as input:
```
grep -rln "FEATURE_MATRIX.md" --include='*.py' --include='*.sh' --include='*.yml' .
-> scripts/parity/matrix_generator.py       (writes it — the generator)
   tests/parity/test_matrix_generation.py   (skips the test if file absent)

                                              uploads/links the fresh copy)
```
`docs/parity/README.md` still mentions the filename in its own docs, which is
fine since `matrix_generator.py` still produces it on demand — only the
stale *checked-in* copy was the problem. `CHANGELOG.md`'s mention is a
historical record of a past release and was left untouched.

**Final consistency check**:
```
grep -n "18/18\|/18\b\|all 18 patterns" README.md
```
Every remaining hit is now internally consistent (6 languages "all 18
patterns," C#/Java/Scala explicitly "17 of 18" / "17 actual") — no
contradictions remain.

items.title: Split the README; fix the version the CLI reports; release 0.4.1
items.body:
## The audit, re-run

Old numbers were stale — the README had grown since. Current: **2,420 words** (not the 2,202 previously reported), 17 headings, **three Diátaxis types** against a threshold of two, and **rung 2 absent**. Siblings finished at 1,075 and 1,007.

## Split, not trimmed — nothing deleted

- `docs/commands.md` — reference: every sub-command, the pipeline diagram, what the foundry does
- `docs/getting-started.md` — how-to: install, dev setup, reproducing the headline table
- README keeps explanation + the ladder. **1,125 words.**

**Rung 2 written.** It was simply absent — a reader could learn what the project measured without learning who should care. Now: a robust model and an exhausted benchmark both report "0% of attacks succeeded", and the success rate alone cannot tell them apart. Question-before-finding ordering preserved.

## Step 7 found a live defect

`redteam version` printed **0.3.0** while the package was 0.4.0. `pyproject.toml` was bumped for that release and the hardcoded `__version__` was not. Confirmed in the **published wheel**: `METADATA: Version: 0.4.0` beside `redteam/__init__.py: 0.3.0`. Every earlier release kept them in step by hand; 0.4.0 is where that failed, and it shipped.

**There was a test:**

```python
def test_package_version_is_set() -> None:
    assert __version__ == "0.3.0"
```

A third hardcoded copy. Green throughout the release, because the code and the test held the same wrong value and agreed with each other while the package metadata said something else. Its neighbour asserted `__version__ in result.stdout` — the code compared to itself.

**Agreement is not correctness**, arrived at a third time today. Fixed by removing the copies rather than synchronising them: `__version__` reads installed distribution metadata; `tests/unit/test_version.py` compares it against `pyproject.toml`, the installed distribution, and the CLI's own output, and refuses to run against the not-installed placeholder. Recorded as instance #14.

## Two more stale counts

The Documentation table called the absence catalogue "Nine metrics" when it held thirteen; `docs/ROADMAP.md` said "Phase 0 is complete" while every phase was done. Both replaced with descriptions rather than corrected counts — a count in a link description decays every time the target grows.

## Instance #13 reclassified

The rebuild gap moves from an open item to a **stated property**. Closing it would mean uploading locally-built artifacts, which needs a token that deliberately does not exist and would bypass every guard in `publish.yml`. What is common to both is the source tree, which is verified. Filing it as open implied someone should close it; nobody should.

## 0.4.1

**Patch.** No API change, no behaviour change beyond a version string that now reports the truth. It needs a version at all only because a PyPI description is frozen at upload and the description *is* the README.

No release is performed by this PR.

# Summary

The README's benchmark charts, matrix table and prose predated the optimization round that merged in #1 — several claims had inverted (e.g. "the pure-Go core is slower than native OpenCV single-threaded on every scene": it now **wins on every scene**). This PR makes the numbers self-maintaining and fixes the stale text.

## Auto-generation pipeline

- **`docs/collect.py`** parses the raw outputs — `go test -bench . -benchtime 5x -cpu 1,4` (both cores), `bench/cpp/native_bench`, memprobe peak-RSS lines, native 1080p VmHWM — into **`docs/benchdata.json`** (partial re-measurements merge per field, so the dataset stays coherent).

- **`.github/workflows/bench-charts.yml`** re-measures all three implementations in one session on every push to `main` (and on manual dispatch), regenerates everything, and commits the refresh with `[skip ci]` — so charts always describe the code on `main`, measured on one machine in one session. Native peak RSS is sampled from `/proc/<pid>/status` VmHWM (no GNU `time` dependency).

## Fresh coherent dataset included

Seeded with a full same-machine session on the optimized code (4-vCPU Xeon 2.80 GHz, this container): native OpenCV C++ built from the same prebuilt static 4.12 archives the CI uses, both Go cores at `-cpu 1,4`, all memory probes. items.title: docs(0051): say only what is true, and let CI keep it that way
items.body:
ADR 0051's release bar is that nothing **actively misleads**. Measured against it, the README oversold in five places, and the two evaluation documents mis-attributed limitations to tasks that do not cover them.

## Claims softened to what is actually known

- **"linear horizontal scalability"** (headline + Principles) — unmeasured. ADR 0048 T3 is `planned`, and that ADR forbids measuring a scaling curve on one host. The honest form is a statement about the architecture: shared-nothing, no coordinator on the publish hot path, curve not yet measured. Same for the shared-subscriptions line billing itself as "the linear-scaling lever".
- **"The main thing not yet done is cutting a tagged release"** — not true. It now points at a new **Limitations** section listing what a reader would otherwise discover in production.

## Numbers that were wrong

| | was | is |
|---|---|---|
| peer frame encode | ~280 ns | **~439 ns** |
| peer frame decode | ~420 ns | **~357 ns** |
| ADR count | 44 | **55** |

The peer-frame figures were stale *bincode* numbers, superseded by the postcard re-baseline (`BASELINE.md`). They under-reported encode cost by ~35% **in our own favour**. `mqtt-bridge` and `mqttd-operator` were absent from the crate table entirely.

## Limitations attributed to the wrong task

`SIZING.md` and `COMPARISON.md` both cited **0041-T7** for the missing per-store disk quota. T7 is the *bridge-spool* byte bound — the per-store quota was tracked by nothing. SIZING further claimed all four unbounded axes were "tracked as T6–T8" when two were tracked by no task at all.

The clauses were kept and the tasks created:

- **0041-T9** — per-store disk bound: one store can consume the whole watermark and brown out the others.
- **0041-T10** — per-connection write buffering. `MAX_BACKLOG` is a **hard-coded 10 000 messages** per stalled subscriber: bounded in count, unbounded in bytes, and not configurable by any setting. At the 1 MiB default packet size that is **~10 GiB of worst-case headroom per connection**. Now stated plainly in README, SIZING and COMPARISON, with the practical mitigation — cap `MQTTD_MAX_PACKET_SIZE`, since the product of the two is the real worst case.

## Two claims about other people, and about ourselves

- `COMPARISON.md` published a **competitor-negative benchmark observation** (NanoMQ QoS-1 acks stalling at 1024 msgs/connection) sourced from a harness whose own rules forbid publishing dev-grade numbers. Ours is the honesty rule; breaking it against a third party is worse than breaking it about ourselves. **Removed.**
- `COMPARISON.md` still said **"no operator by decision"** — stale since ADR 0055 was accepted and an operator was built. It now says what is true: built and e2e-tested, *not packaged for installation*, chart is the supported path.
- `deploy/operator/operator.yaml` now declares itself **development/e2e only**. It pins `mqttd-operator:e2e` with `imagePullPolicy: Never`, so outside kind every pod sits in `ErrImageNeverPull` forever. A manifest that merely *looked* installable would be the more expensive mistake.

## And the derivable facts are now CI-enforced

`scripts/check-readme-facts.py` (**ADR 0051 T1**) checks the two README facts that have a mechanical source of truth — the ADR count and the crate table — because those drift silently: nothing fails when a crate is added or an ADR is written.

Verified by reintroducing both real defects:

```
README states facts the tree contradicts:
  - claims 44 ADRs; docs/adr/ holds 55
  - crate `mqtt-bridge` is missing from the Workspace layout table
```

Wired into the existing `delivery dashboard` job. `gen-status.py --check` green; every README ADR link resolves.

## Not included

The **MSRV statement**. `rust-version` (1.88; operator 1.89) and `rust-toolchain.toml` (1.97.0) are different things and not actually in conflict — but *nothing verifies the MSRV*: every CI job uses `stable` or the 1.97 pin, so "1.88" is an untested claim. That needs a verification job, not a sentence, and follows separately.

items.title: ci: dependabot + benchmark auto-refresh (auto-open PRs)
items.body:
Two automations that open PRs on their own — no manual upkeep.

## 1. Dependabot (`.github/dependabot.yml`)
Weekly PRs for:
- **CLI npm deps** — `typescript`, `@types/node` (dir `/packages/cli`)
- **GitHub Actions versions** — `actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-node`, etc.

Commit prefixes `build:` / `ci:`, capped at 5 open PRs each, labeled `dependencies`.

## 2. Benchmark auto-refresh (`.github/workflows/benchmark-refresh.yml`)
Weekly (Mon 06:00 UTC) + manual `workflow_dispatch`. Reruns `npm run bench`; if `docs/benchmarks/README.md` drifted, pushes `bot/benchmark-refresh` and opens a PR with the fresh numbers (skips if one's already open).

This is the other half of the CI drift gate: CI **fails** a PR whose committed benchmark is stale; this **produces the fix**. So the published token numbers stay honest as the compiler evolves, hands-off.

Built-in `gh` CLI only — no third-party actions, in keeping with the zero-dependency ethos. Both YAML files validated locally.
